planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; reticulata iris needs a dry summer dormancy and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil, performing best in a rock garden or raised bed.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; reticulata iris needs a dry summer dormancy and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil, performing best in a rock garden or raised bed. One of the earliest and most popular dwarf bulbous iris cultivars, it produces rich royal-blue flowers with a bright yellow-ridged blaze on the falls, opening low to the ground among grassy foliage in very early spring, often blooming through a late snow before crocuses have even started. Its diminutive scale and intense, saturated color make it a favorite for edging a rock garden, tucking among stepping stones, or naturalizing under deciduous shrubs where its early bloom is not shaded out before the shrub leafs out. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom before removing it, and avoid summer irrigation, which can rot the small bulbs during dormancy.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; reticulata iris needs a dry summer dormancy and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil, performing best in a rock garden or raised bed.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; reticulata iris needs a dry summer dormancy and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil, performing best in a rock garden or raised bed. A hybrid between two dwarf iris species, this uniquely marked cultivar produces pale, luminous, ice-blue and pale yellow flowers netted with fine gray-blue veining, an intricate, almost translucent pattern quite unlike the solid deep blue of most other reticulata iris, opening low to the ground in very early spring. One of the most popular and widely photographed small bulb cultivars for its unusual, subtle color pattern, it naturalizes readily in favorable rock garden conditions once its exacting drainage requirements are met. Allow foliage to die back naturally before removing it, and avoid any summer moisture, which quickly rots the small bulbs during their required dry dormancy.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; this species iris blooms extremely early, sometimes emerging through snow, and needs a dry summer dormancy to persist.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; this species iris blooms extremely early, sometimes emerging through snow, and needs a dry summer dormancy to persist. Large, richly patterned deep blue to violet flowers with white, gold-flecked markings on the falls open remarkably early, often the very first bulb to flower in late winter, well ahead of crocus and even before its own grassy foliage has fully developed. Native to the mountains of Turkey, it is the wild species behind many of the popular reticulata iris hybrids more commonly sold, and grows and multiplies well in a rock garden or raised bed with the same sharp drainage its hybrid offspring require. Allow foliage to mature and yellow naturally after bloom before removing it, and avoid summer watering, which is fatal to the bulbs during their dry dormant season.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Pickwick crocus naturalizes well in a lawn or border and multiplies steadily by cormlets over the years.

directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Pickwick crocus naturalizes well in a lawn or border and multiplies steadily by cormlets over the years. Large, goblet-shaped flowers are boldly striped in silvery-lilac and deep purple with a bright orange center, one of the largest-flowered and most strikingly patterned of the classic large-flowering Dutch crocus cultivars, opening wide in full sun each early spring day and closing again at dusk or on cloudy days. Long popular for naturalizing in lawns, where its foliage dies back and disappears before the grass needs its first mowing, it multiplies steadily over the years by producing small cormlets around the parent corm. Allow foliage to die back naturally before mowing over a naturalized planting, and divide congested clumps in summer dormancy if flowering begins to decline.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Ruby Giant crocus blooms earlier than large-flowered Dutch crocus and naturalizes readily in a lawn or rock garden.

directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Ruby Giant crocus blooms earlier than large-flowered Dutch crocus and naturalizes readily in a lawn or rock garden. Deep reddish-purple flowers with a bright orange throat open early in the crocus season, ahead of the larger Dutch crocus hybrids, on a compact species-type crocus that multiplies vigorously by both cormlets and self-sown seed to form expanding drifts over the years. Its early bloom time and rich, saturated purple color make it a strong choice for an early-season naturalized planting in a lawn, rock garden, or woodland edge, providing critical early nectar for the first bees active in late winter and early spring. Allow foliage to die back naturally before mowing over any naturalized planting, and let the crocus self-sow freely to build a larger colony over time.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; White Triumphator is a classic lily-flowered tulip prized for cut-flower use and elegant border display.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; White Triumphator is a classic lily-flowered tulip prized for cut-flower use and elegant border display. Tall, elegant, pure white flowers with gracefully pointed, recurving petals open in a refined, lily-like form quite different from the rounder cup shape of standard Darwin hybrid tulips, on tall, sturdy stems that make it one of the most widely used white tulips for both garden display and cut-flower arrangements. Its clean, classic color and elegant flower shape have made it a mainstay of white and monochromatic spring garden designs, pairing well with blue muscari and other spring bulbs for a refined, coordinated display. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom before removing it, and treat as an annual after the first year in warm climates, since most hybrid tulips decline and rebloom poorly after their initial spring display.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Salome daffodil naturalizes well and its trumpet color changes distinctly as the flower matures.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Salome daffodil naturalizes well and its trumpet color changes distinctly as the flower matures. Broad, overlapping white petals surround a trumpet that opens soft yellow and gradually fades through apricot to a soft peachy pink as the flower ages, a striking color transformation that means a single planting shows several different trumpet shades at once across flowers of different ages. This large-cupped daffodil is a long-standing garden favorite for its unusual, evolving pink coloring, naturalizing well into larger clumps over the years in a border or lightly shaded woodland planting. Let the foliage die back naturally after bloom before removing it, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer once dormant.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jetfire is an early-blooming, cyclamineus-type daffodil that naturalizes readily and is one of the most reliable early-season daffodils.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jetfire is an early-blooming, cyclamineus-type daffodil that naturalizes readily and is one of the most reliable early-season daffodils. Bright golden-yellow petals sweep dramatically backward away from a long, strongly contrasting orange-red trumpet, a bold, swept-back flower form typical of the cyclamineus daffodil group, opening among the very earliest daffodils each spring on compact, sturdy stems well suited to a rock garden, container, or the front of a border. One of the most popular and widely planted small daffodil cultivars for its vivid bicolor contrast and reliable early bloom, it naturalizes readily into larger clumps and provides an early nectar source for the season's first bees. Let foliage die back naturally after bloom before removing it, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer once dormant.
